case_title: Sheo Shankar Singh v. State of Jharkhand & Anr.
accused_victim_relationship: Political/land rival and prior enmity: the deceased, a sitting MLA, opposed the accused's coal-theft activities and helped restore a petrol pump against the accused's family's interests (as the court accepted)
statutory_provisions: Charged: IPC s.302, s.34, s.120B, s.201; Arms Act s.27 (Umesh Singh). Convictions for appellants: IPC s.302 r/w s.34; Arms Act s.27 (Umesh Singh)
weapon: Pistol (9 mm bullets; empty cartridges recovered from scene)
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony (two eyewitnesses); identification (court and test identification parade); recovery/seizure (motorcycles, cartridges, blood-stained clothing); medical evidence; motive evidence; post-mortem
aggravating_circumstances: Killing of a sitting MLA by gunfire at close range; a further shot fired at the victim on the ground; body pushed down roadside slope
mitigating_circumstances: Accused not professional killers; no political angle to killing; nothing particularly brutal in manner of execution; difference of opinion on sentence between trial court and High Court
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for life; Umesh Singh additionally convicted under Arms Act s.27 and sentenced to three years rigorous imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Convictions upheld; life sentence enhanced to death sentence; revision seeking enhancement allowed
offence_finally_established: Murder under IPC s.302 r/w s.34 (both appellants); Arms Act s.27 (Umesh Singh)
neutral_facts: On an afternoon in April 2000, the victim, a sitting state legislator, was riding as a pillion passenger on a motorcycle driven by an informant on a road near a coal-handling site. The informant heard a gunshot from behind and saw a black motorcycle without a registration number running alongside on the left. It was driven by the accused, with a second man on the pillion holding a pistol. The pillion rider fired at close range; the victim was struck in the head, slumped onto the informant, and both men fell to the road. The driver stopped a short distance ahead. The second man walked back, threatened the informant to leave, fired another shot at the victim, pushed the body down the roadside slope, and both men rode away towards a nearby town. Two bystanders who arrived afterwards stated that they had earlier seen the accused riding the same unregistered motorcycle with a pillion passenger in the area. The informant's motorcycle was seized from the scene. A second black unregistered motorcycle was seized from premises linked to the accused; its registration certificate was in another person's name. Two 9 mm empty cartridges were recovered from the scene. The informant's blood-stained T-shirt and torn jeans were seized. A medical examination that evening recorded injuries consistent with a fall. The post-mortem recorded gunshot wounds to the head as the cause of death. The informant identified the pillion rider in court, and one bystander identified him in a test identification parade. Investigators did not send the clothing to a forensic laboratory or the cartridges to a ballistics expert, and the weapon was never recovered. Evidence of a dispute over a petrol pump and of the victim's action against coal theft was also given.
offence_severity: Death or imprisonment for life (as described in the judgment; life imprisonment is the normal rule and death an exception); no fine or minimum stated
physical_harm: Victim died of gunshot wounds to the head (multiple entry and exit wounds). The eyewitness suffered abrasions and injuries when he fell from the motorcycle.
number_of_offences: 5 charged (IPC ss.302, 34, 120B, 201; Arms Act s.27); 2 finally upheld for the appellants (IPC s.302 r/w s.34 for both; Arms Act s.27 for Umesh Singh)
motive: Accepted by the court: the accused were part of a coal mafia; the victim, an MLA, opposed coal theft and helped restore a petrol pump to a complainant, which annoyed the accused and their family. The victim was perceived as a hurdle to their activities.
key_evidence_accepted: Eyewitness accounts of PW16 and PW6; PW1 and PW2 sightings of accused on the motorcycle and PW1 test identification of Umesh Singh; seizure of motorcycles, cartridges, blood-stained clothing; medical evidence of PW16's injuries; prompt FIR; motive evidence from PW15, PW16 and PW19
witness_credibility: PW16 found consistent and reliable by both courts, with no enmity or bias shown; PW1 and PW2 corroborated his presence; PW6 accepted despite a month-and-a-half delay in recording his statement, as the investigating officer's explanation was accepted; PW1's identification accepted
post_offence_conduct: Fled the scene on the motorcycle after the shooting, per the accepted eyewitness account; no surrender or disclosure noted
trial_duration: offence: 14 April 2000; trial judgment: 18 November 2003 (guilt), 20 November 2003 (sentence order); High Court: 6 May 2005; Supreme Court: 15 February 2011
legal_representation: Accused: U.R. Lalit (senior counsel) with others; State/respondents: A.T.M. Rangaramanujam and Sunil Kumar (senior counsel)
investigation_status: FIR registered (Police Station Govindpur); investigation completed; charge-sheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: No reference made to forensic laboratory for blood-stained T-shirt or to ballistics expert for cartridges; PW16 not put through a test identification parade; month-and-a-half delay in recording PW6's statement
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted, life imprisonment. High Court: convictions upheld, sentence enhanced to death. Supreme Court: convictions affirmed, death sentence commuted to life imprisonment
defence_argument: Failure to hold a test identification parade for PW16 casts doubt on his identification of Umesh Singh; PW16 could not have looked back while driving; PW6 was not an eyewitness and his statement was delayed; no forensic or ballistic examination; motorcycle borrowing not corroborated; FIR lodging doubted; death sentence not warranted
legal_principle_applied: Motive recedes where eyewitness testimony is credible but supports the case if proved; TIP is corroboration only and its absence does not weaken in-court identification; mere delay in examining a witness is not fatal; investigative lapses do not justify total rejection; rarest of rare test for death penalty
precedent_relied_upon: Shivaji Genu Mohite (1973) 3 SCC 219; Hari Shanker (1996) 9 SCC 40; Kishanpal (2008) 16 SCC 73; Malkhansingh (2003) 5 SCC 746; Pramod Mandal (2004) 13 SCC 150; Aqeel Ahmad (2008) 16 SCC 372; Ranbir (1973) 2 SCC 444; Satbir Singh (2009) 13 SCC 790; Ram Bihari Yadav (1998) 4 SCC 517; Surendra Paswan (2003) 12 SCC 360; Amar Singh (2003) 2 SCC 518; Jagmohan Singh (1973) 1 SCC 20; Bachan Singh (1980) 2 SCC 684; Machhi Singh (1983) 3 SCC 470; Farooq (2002) 4 SCC 697; Santosh Kumar Bariyar (2009) 6 SCC 498; Prakash Sakha Vasave (2009) 11 SCC 193
sentencing_rationale: High Court not justified in imposing death: accused not professional killers; no political angle; nothing particularly brutal in execution; trial court did not find rarest of rare case; death commuted to life imprisonment
judicial_mitigating_factors: Accused not professional killers; no political angle to the killing; nothing particularly brutal, grotesque or diabolical in execution; difference of opinion on sentence between trial court and High Court
judicial_aggravating_factors: None found sufficient to justify death; the court noted the killing as inhuman but found no aggravating feature amounting to the rarest of rare
